lead: When bending, shear and torsion act together, their stresses add. IS 456 avoids a complex interaction formula: it turns factored torque T<sub>u</sub> into an equivalent moment M<sub>t</sub> and an equivalent shear V<sub>e</sub>. Flexural steel is designed for M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>, stirrups for V<sub>e</sub>, and the section is checked for equivalent shear stress. Edge beams, spandrel beams, curved girders and eccentrically loaded beams need this. Only a few universities teach it as a separate advanced chapter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.3 for Mt and Ve, Chapter 3.2 for stirrups, and Unit 2 for flexural design.

blocks.text: Torsion creates shear stresses around the perimeter. Bending shear also creates shear stress. IS 456 replaces torque by two ordinary actions, so familiar flexure and shear design can be used.

blocks.where: T<sub>u</sub> is factored torque in kN·m; b is width in mm; D is overall depth in mm; M<sub>t</sub> is equivalent moment in kN·m.
V<sub>u</sub> is factored shear in kN; b is width in m when T<sub>u</sub> is in kN·m; V<sub>e</sub> is equivalent shear in kN.

blocks.text: The factors 1.7 and 1.6 are calibrated. This is not a simple addition of actions. After design, check τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d) ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub>. Here τ<sub>ve</sub> is equivalent shear stress in MPa, b and d are in mm, V<sub>e</sub> is in N, and τ<sub>c,max</sub> comes from IS 456 Table 20. If τ<sub>ve</sub> is close to τ<sub>c,max</sub>, deepen the beam rather than crowd stirrups.

items: Find factored M<sub>u</sub>, V<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>u</sub>. Use T<sub>u</sub> in kN·m and b in m for V<sub>e</sub>.
Compute M<sub>t</sub> and V<sub>e</sub>. Design longitudinal steel for M<sub>d</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub> by Unit 2; put bars at corners and side faces.
Design closed stirrups for Ve, not Vu, using Chapter 3.2.
Check τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d) ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub>. If it fails, enlarge the section or raise concrete grade.
Detail corner bars, side-face steel and loops as in Chapter 3.7.

blocks.text: Torsion shear reverses around the perimeter, so closed stirrups and corner bars are essential. The equivalent method is conservative; it lets a designer use ordinary beam charts. Torsion still controls detailing. Torsion cracks spiral around the beam, so longitudinal bars need end anchorage and closed stirrups need proper hooks. Some syllabi call this design for combined bending, shear and torsion.

figure.caption: How factored torsion T<sub>u</sub> becomes M<sub>t</sub> and V<sub>e</sub>, and how the final design uses M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub> and V<sub>e</sub>. Notice torsion feeds both the moment and the stirrup design.

spec.aria: Bending M, shear V and torsion T combine: T becomes M_t and V_e, and final design uses M plus M_t and V_e.

examples.question: A beam has b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, d = 550 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kN·m, V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m. Take M25 concrete with τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 MPa. Find M<sub>d</sub>, V<sub>e</sub> and τ<sub>ve</sub>, and check the section.
steps: 1.70 ≤ 3.1 MPa, so section is adequate; design steel for 202.94 kN·m and stirrups for 280 kN.
examples.answer: M<sub>d</sub> = 202.94 kN·m, V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN and τ<sub>ve</sub> = 1.70 MPa; τ<sub>ve</sub> < τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 MPa.
examples.check:
b = 300
D = 600
d = 550
Mu = 150
Vu = 120
Tu = 30
Mt = Tu * (1 + D / b) / 1.7
Md = Mu + Mt
Ve = Vu + 1.6 * Tu / (b / 1000)
tau = Ve * 1000 / (b * d)
print(round(Mt, 2))
print(round(Md, 2))
print(round(Ve, 2))
print(round(tau, 2))

traps: Using b in mm in V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6T<sub>u</sub>/b when T<sub>u</sub> is in kN·m. Convert b to metres.
Designing stirrups only for V<sub>u</sub>. Use V<sub>e</sub>.
Swapping b and D in the M<sub>t</sub> formula.
Skipping the τ<sub>c,max</sub> check after torsion is added.
Adding M<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>t</sub> with different units.

quiz.q: Write the expressions for M<sub>t</sub> and V<sub>e</sub>.
Why is M<sub>t</sub> added to M<sub>u</sub> instead of adding T<sub>u</sub> directly?
quiz.a: Torsion is converted to an equivalent bending demand that flexural steel can resist.

quiz.q: b = 250 mm, D = 500 mm, T<sub>u</sub> = 20 kN·m, V<sub>u</sub> = 80 kN. Find M<sub>t</sub> and V<sub>e</sub>.
τ<sub>ve</sub> = 3.4 MPa on M25 concrete. What action is needed?
quiz.a: It exceeds τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 MPa; enlarge the section or use higher-grade concrete, not only more stirrups.

quiz.q: V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN, b = 300 mm, d = 550 mm. Find τ<sub>ve</sub>.
Why are closed stirrups used for torsion?
quiz.a: Torsion shear acts around the perimeter; a closed loop resists it on all faces.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, software checks combined actions with interaction surfaces and strut-and-tie models rather than one equivalent-load formula. Bridge and curved-girder design often uses space truss models for torsion. Researchers test reinforced concrete under combined bending, shear and torsion to calibrate code factors.
